verse.text: Paul, an apostle—not from people nor through a person, but through Jesus Christ and God the Father, who raised him from the dead—
and all the brothers and sisters who are with me, to the assemblies of Galatia:
verse.note: The Greek word was the ordinary term for a civic gathering and, in the Greek Old Testament, for Israel assembled before God. “Church” is the near-universal rendering and readers know what it refers to, but it now suggests a building or an institution. This translation uses “assembly” throughout so that the reader can see it is one Greek word.

verse.text: Grace to you and peace from God the Father and our Lord Jesus Christ,
who gave himself for our sins to rescue us from the present evil age, according to the will of our God and Father,
to whom be the glory forever and ever. Amen.
I am astonished that you are so quickly turning away from the one who called you in the grace of Christ to a different good news—
verse.note: The Greek noun was an everyday word for the public announcement of good news, used also of imperial proclamations. “Gospel” is the traditional rendering, but it has become a religious term and a book title. The related verb in verses 8, 9, 11, 16 and 23 is rendered “announce good news” so that the connection stays visible.

verse.text: not that there is another; there are only some people who are troubling you and want to distort the good news of Christ.
But even if we or an angel from heaven should announce good news to you contrary to the good news we announced to you, let that one be accursed.
verse.note: The Greek word is “anathema”. In the Greek Old Testament it translates the Hebrew term for something irrevocably handed over to God, usually for destruction. Paul is calling down God’s judgment, not merely expressing disapproval or proposing expulsion from the community.

verse.text: As we have said before, so now I say again: if anyone is announcing good news to you contrary to what you received, let that one be accursed.
For am I now trying to win the approval of people, or of God? Or am I seeking to please people? If I were still pleasing people, I would not be a slave of Christ.
verse.note: The verb normally means “persuade” or “win over”. Most translations take it here in the sense of seeking favor, parallel to “please” in the next question. Some interpreters keep “persuade” and read the question as a retort to the charge that Paul tailors his message to his audience.

The Greek word denotes a person owned by a master, not a hired servant. Most English versions soften it to “servant”. The Greek Old Testament also uses the word as a title of honor for Moses, David and the prophets as God’s slaves, and both associations may be present.

verse.text: For I want you to know, brothers and sisters, that the good news announced by me is not of human origin;
for I did not receive it from any person, nor was I taught it, but it came through a revelation of Jesus Christ.
verse.note: The Greek can mean a revelation given by Jesus Christ or a revelation in which Jesus Christ was the one revealed. Verse 16, where God reveals his Son, favors the second, but the contrast with receiving it “from any person” suits the first. The English “of” leaves both open, as the Greek does.

verse.text: For you have heard of my former way of life in Judaism, how I persecuted the assembly of God beyond all measure and tried to destroy it,
verse.note: This rare word appears in the New Testament only here and in verse 14. In earlier Jewish writing in Greek it named the Jewish way of life as something to be zealously defended against foreign pressure. Paul is describing a militant devotion to ancestral custom, not a religion set over against “Christianity”, a contrast that did not yet exist.

verse.text: and I was advancing in Judaism beyond many of my own age among my people, being far more zealous for the traditions of my ancestors.
But when the one who set me apart from my mother’s womb and called me through his grace was pleased

note.term: the one who set me apart

verse.note: Many manuscripts read “God, who set me apart”. The Greek text translated here lacks the word “God”, which was probably added by copyists to make the subject explicit. The meaning is not affected. The language echoes the calls of Isaiah’s servant and of Jeremiah, both chosen from the womb.

verse.text: to reveal his Son in me, so that I might announce the good news about him among the Gentiles, I did not at once consult with flesh and blood,
verse.note: The Greek phrase can mean “in me” (an inward revelation), “to me” (a simple indirect object, as some translations have it), or “through me” (to others by way of Paul). The wording here follows the most literal sense. The same phrase in verse 24 is rendered “because of me”.

The Greek word means “peoples” or “nations”. In the plural, in Jewish usage, it means the non-Jewish peoples. This translation uses “Gentiles” for that sense and “nations” where peoples as such are meant, but it is a single Greek word in both cases.

verse.text: nor did I go up to Jerusalem to those who were apostles before me, but I went away into Arabia, and returned again to Damascus.
verse.note: In Paul’s day “Arabia” meant chiefly the Nabataean kingdom, which stretched south and east of Damascus and had its capital at Petra. It does not necessarily mean the distant Arabian peninsula. Paul does not say what he did there.

verse.text: Then after three years I went up to Jerusalem to get to know Cephas, and I stayed with him fifteen days;
verse.note: Cephas is the Aramaic form of the name Peter; both mean “rock”. Paul usually calls him by the Aramaic name. Some later manuscripts substitute “Peter” here.

verse.text: but I did not see any other of the apostles, except James, the Lord’s brother.
verse.note: The Greek can mean that James was the only other apostle Paul saw, which counts James as an apostle. It can also mean that Paul saw no other apostle, though he did see James. Most interpreters prefer the first reading, but the grammar does not settle it.

verse.text: As to what I am writing to you—look, before God, I am not lying.
Then I went into the regions of Syria and Cilicia.
I remained unknown by sight to the assemblies of Judea that are in Christ;
they only kept hearing, “The one who once persecuted us is now announcing the good news of the faith he once tried to destroy,”
and they glorified God because of me.
Then after fourteen years I went up again to Jerusalem with Barnabas, taking Titus along as well.

I went up in response to a revelation, and I laid before them the good news that I proclaim among the Gentiles—but privately, before those of repute—for fear that I might be running, or had run, in vain.
verse.note: The traditional rendering is “gospel,” which today sounds like a religious term or the title of a book. The Greek was an ordinary word for an announcement of good news, used also of public and imperial proclamations. Many modern translations alternate between “gospel” and “good news.”

verse.text: But not even Titus, who was with me, though he was a Greek, was compelled to be circumcised.
But because of the false brothers secretly brought in, who slipped in to spy on the freedom we have in Christ Jesus, so that they might enslave us—

note.term: so that they might enslave us—

verse.note: Paul’s sentence breaks off here without a main clause, and the translation leaves it broken as the Greek does. Readers must supply something like “the issue arose” or “pressure was applied.” It is disputed whether the “false brothers” were the reason for the Jerusalem visit or people who intervened during it.

verse.text: to them we did not yield in submission even for a moment, so that the truth of the good news might remain with you.
As for those reputed to be something—whatever they were makes no difference to me; God shows no partiality—those of repute added nothing to me.
On the contrary, when they saw that I had been entrusted with the good news for the uncircumcised, just as Peter had been for the circumcised,
for the one who was at work in Peter for an apostleship to the circumcised was also at work in me for the Gentiles,

and when they recognized the grace given to me, James and Cephas and John, who were reputed to be pillars, gave me and Barnabas the right hand of partnership, so that we should go to the Gentiles and they to the circumcised.
verse.note: Cephas is the Aramaic form of the nickname given to Simon; Peter is its Greek equivalent, and both mean “rock.” Paul uses both names in this chapter (Peter in verses 7–8) for the same man.

Most translations have “the right hand of fellowship.” The Greek word means having something in common and was used of business partnerships as well as friendship. Here the handshake seals a working agreement about who goes to whom, so “partnership” was chosen; the word also implies mutual recognition.

verse.text: They asked only that we remember the poor, the very thing I was eager to do.
But when Cephas came to Antioch, I opposed him to his face, because he stood condemned.
For before certain people came from James, he used to eat with the Gentiles; but when they came, he began to draw back and separate himself, fearing those of the circumcision.
verse.note: The phrase is literally “those from circumcision.” It may mean Jewish believers who insisted that Gentile converts be circumcised, which is why many translations say “the circumcision party” or “group.” It may also mean Jews more broadly, whose reaction Peter feared. The translation leaves the phrase open.

verse.text: And the rest of the Jews joined him in this hypocrisy, so that even Barnabas was carried away by their hypocrisy.

But when I saw that they were not walking straight in line with the truth of the good news, I said to Cephas in front of everyone, “If you, though a Jew, live like a Gentile and not like a Jew, how can you compel the Gentiles to live like Jews?”
verse.note: Greek manuscripts have no quotation marks, and it is unclear where Paul’s words to Cephas end. Some translations carry the speech through verse 21; others, as here, close it at verse 14 and take verses 15–21 as Paul’s reflection addressed to the Galatians. The argument flows continuously either way.

verse.text: We are Jews by birth and not sinners from among the Gentiles,

yet we know that a person is not justified by works of the law but only through faith in Jesus Christ. So we too believed in Christ Jesus, in order to be justified by faith in Christ and not by works of the law, because by works of the law no flesh will be justified.
verse.note: Greek has one word-family where English has two: “justify” here and “righteousness” in verse 21 share a single root, as do “just” and “righteous.” To be “justified” is to be declared or set in the right. Some scholars prefer “justice” or “vindicate” to keep the link visible in English.

The law in view is the law of Moses. The traditional understanding is that “works of the law” means deeds done in obedience to its commandments generally. Many recent scholars think Paul has especially in mind the practices that marked Jews off from Gentiles—circumcision, food laws, and Sabbath—which are the issues at stake in this chapter. The closing words of the verse echo Psalm 143:2.

The Greek is literally “faith of Jesus Christ,” and “faith of Christ” later in the verse. The traditional and still majority reading is “faith in Christ,” meaning the believer’s trust. A substantial body of scholars reads it as “the faithfulness of Jesus Christ,” meaning his own faithful obedience. The grammar allows both.

verse.text: But if, while seeking to be justified in Christ, we ourselves were also found to be sinners, is Christ then a servant of sin? By no means!
For if I build up again the very things I tore down, I show myself to be a transgressor.
For through the law I died to the law, so that I might live to God. I have been crucified with Christ,
and it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me. The life I now live in the flesh I live by faith in the Son of God, who loved me and gave himself up for me.

note.term: faith in the Son of God
note.traditional: faith in the Son of God

verse.note: As in verse 16, the Greek is literally “faith of the Son of God.” It can also be read as “the faithfulness of the Son of God,” which would connect naturally with the words that follow about his love and self-giving. The majority reading is followed here.

verse.text: I do not set aside the grace of God; for if righteousness comes through the law, then Christ died for nothing.
You foolish Galatians! Who has bewitched you—you before whose eyes Jesus Christ was publicly portrayed as crucified?
This is the only thing I want to learn from you: did you receive the Spirit by works of the Law or by hearing with faith?
verse.note: The Greek is literally “hearing of faith.” The first noun can mean the act of hearing or the thing heard (a message or report), and “faith” can be the act of believing or what is believed. The phrase may therefore mean “believing what you heard” or “the message that calls for faith.” The rendering takes it as hearing accompanied by faith, set against “works.”

verse.text: Are you so foolish? Having begun by the Spirit, are you now finishing by the flesh?
Have you suffered so much for nothing—if it really was for nothing?
verse.note: The verb can mean simply “experience,” and some translations read “Did you experience so much for nothing?”, referring to the Spirit and the deeds of power just mentioned. Everywhere else in the New Testament the verb means to suffer something bad, and the rendering follows that usage. The letter does not otherwise say what the Galatians suffered, so the question remains open.

verse.text: So then, does the one who supplies you with the Spirit and works deeds of power among you do it by works of the Law or by hearing with faith?
verse.note: The Greek is the ordinary word for “power,” used in the plural for acts that display it. “Miracles” is a fully acceptable rendering and the meaning is not disputed. “Deeds of power” is used throughout this translation so that the link with the word “power” stays visible.

verse.text: Just so, Abraham “believed God, and it was credited to him as righteousness.”
verse.note: Paul quotes Genesis 15:6. Greek has a single word family where English has two: “righteous” and “just,” “righteousness” and “justice,” and the verb “justify” (verses 8, 11, 24) all share one root. A Greek reader would hear “righteousness,” “the righteous one,” and “justify” in this chapter as the same word in different forms. Some scholars prefer “justice” in English.

verse.text: Understand, then, that those who are of faith—these are sons of Abraham.

note.traditional: children of Abraham; sons of Abraham

verse.note: The Greek word is “sons,” here and in verse 26 (“sons of God”). It is kept because the argument turns on the son as heir (verse 29 and the next chapter). Paul applies it to men and women alike, as verse 28 makes plain. Many translations render it “children” or “descendants.”

verse.text: And the Scripture, foreseeing that God would justify the Gentiles by faith, announced the good news in advance to Abraham: “In you all the nations will be blessed.”
verse.note: “Gentiles” and “nations” in this verse translate the same Greek word, which in the plural means the peoples of the world other than Israel. Paul’s point depends on the identity: the promise to Abraham in Genesis that “all the nations” would be blessed is, for him, a promise about the Gentiles.

verse.text: So then, those who are of faith are blessed along with believing Abraham.
For all who are of works of the Law are under a curse, for it is written: “Cursed is everyone who does not remain in all the things written in the book of the Law, to do them.”
And that no one is justified before God by the Law is clear, because “The righteous one will live by faith.”
But the Law is not of faith; rather, “The one who does these things will live by them.”
Christ redeemed us from the curse of the Law by becoming a curse for us, for it is written, “Cursed is everyone who hangs on a tree.”
This was so that in Christ Jesus the blessing of Abraham might come to the Gentiles, so that we might receive the promise of the Spirit through faith.
Brothers and sisters, I am speaking in human terms: even with a human will, once it has been ratified, no one sets it aside or adds to it.
verse.note: The Greek word here is the same one rendered “covenant” in verse 17. In everyday Greek it meant a person’s last will and testament; in the Greek Old Testament it was the standard word for God’s covenant. Paul plays on both senses, moving from a human will that cannot be altered once ratified to God’s covenant with Abraham and the “inheritance” it brings. Some translations use “covenant” in both verses.

verse.text: Now the promises were spoken to Abraham and to his seed. It does not say, “And to seeds,” as though of many, but as of one, “And to your seed,” who is Christ.
verse.note: “Seed” is the ordinary biblical word for descendants, a singular noun normally used collectively. Paul knows the collective sense (verse 29 applies it to all who belong to Christ). Here he presses the singular form to say the promise finds its goal in one descendant, Christ, in whom the many are included.

verse.text: What I mean is this: the Law, which came four hundred thirty years later, does not invalidate a covenant previously ratified by God, so as to nullify the promise.
For if the inheritance is from the Law, it is no longer from a promise; but God has graciously given it to Abraham through a promise.
Why, then, the Law? It was added because of transgressions, until the seed to whom the promise had been made should come; and it was ordained through angels by the hand of a mediator.
verse.note: The Greek preposition means “for the sake of” or “on account of,” and does not say how the Law relates to transgressions. Interpreters are divided between three readings: to restrain wrongdoing, to identify wrongdoing as a violation of a known command, or even to provoke it. The rendering leaves the question open, as the Greek does.

verse.text: Now a mediator is not for one party alone, but God is one.

note.term: a mediator is not for one party alone
note.traditional: a mediator is not a mediator of one

verse.note: The Greek says literally “the mediator is not of one, but God is one.” The verse is famously obscure and has been explained in many ways. The mediator of verse 19 is Moses, and Jewish tradition held that angels were present at the giving of the Law at Sinai. The most common view is that a law passed through intermediaries is less direct than the promise, which the one God gave to Abraham himself.

verse.text: Is the Law, then, against the promises of God? Certainly not! For if a law had been given that could give life, then righteousness really would have come from the Law.
But the Scripture confined everything under sin, so that the promise might be given by faith in Jesus Christ to those who believe.
verse.note: The Greek is literally “faith of Jesus Christ,” and the grammar allows two readings: faith directed toward Jesus Christ, or the faithfulness shown by Jesus Christ himself. “Faith in Jesus Christ” is the traditional and still majority reading. “The faithfulness of Jesus Christ” has substantial scholarly support, and on that reading the following words, “to those who believe,” are not a repetition.

verse.text: Before faith came, we were held in custody under the Law, confined until the coming faith would be revealed.
So the Law became our guardian until Christ, so that we might be justified by faith.
verse.note: The Greek word names a household slave who escorted a boy to and from school and supervised his behavior until he came of age. He was a minder and disciplinarian, not a teacher, so the older “schoolmaster” and “tutor” mislead. The words “until Christ” can also be read “to lead us to Christ”; the surrounding verses, which speak of a period ending when faith came, favor the sense of time.

verse.text: But now that faith has come, we are no longer under a guardian.
For in Christ Jesus you are all sons of God through faith.
verse.note: The Greek word order is “sons of God through the faith in Christ Jesus.” Traditionally “in Christ Jesus” is taken as the object of faith. Many scholars instead take it separately, as the sphere in which believers are sons, parallel to “one in Christ Jesus” in verse 28. The rendering follows the second view.

verse.text: For all of you who were baptized into Christ have clothed yourselves with Christ.
There is neither Jew nor Greek, there is neither slave nor free, there is no male and female; for you are all one in Christ Jesus.
verse.note: The first two pairs are joined by “nor,” but the third has “and.” The change echoes the wording of the Greek Genesis 1:27, “male and female he made them.” Many translations smooth it to “neither male nor female”; the rendering keeps the shift so that the echo of the creation account can be heard.

verse.text: And if you belong to Christ, then you are Abraham’s seed, heirs according to promise.
What I am saying is this: as long as the heir is a minor, he is no different from a slave, though he is owner of everything,
but he is under guardians and managers until the date set by his father.
So also we, when we were minors, were enslaved under the elements of the world.

note.traditional: elements of the world; elemental spirits; elementary principles

verse.note: The Greek word could mean the basic components of something: the letters of the alphabet, the rudiments of a subject, or the physical elements (earth, water, air, fire) of which the world was thought to be made. In the period, the full phrase “elements of the world” most often refers to those physical elements, which many peoples revered as divine. Other interpreters take it here as “elementary principles” of religion, or as “elemental spirits,” a sense not clearly attested this early. The plain rendering leaves these options open; the same word recurs in verse 9.

verse.text: But when the fullness of time came, God sent out his Son, born of a woman, born under the law,
to redeem those under the law, so that we might receive adoption as sons.

note.traditional: adoption of sons; adoption as sons

verse.note: The word is the ordinary Greek legal term for adoption, a practice familiar in the Roman world, where an adopted son gained full rights of inheritance. “Sons” is kept because the argument turns on inheritance and on the link with God’s own Son; Paul has just said (3:28) that this status belongs to men and women alike.

verse.text: And because you are sons, God sent out the Spirit of his Son into our hearts, crying out, “Abba, Father!”
verse.note: “Abba” is the Aramaic word for “father,” used in address within the family and in prayer. Paul keeps the Aramaic word and sets its Greek equivalent beside it, as also in Romans 8:15 and Mark 14:36.

verse.text: So you are no longer a slave but a son, and if a son, then also an heir through God.
But back then, not knowing God, you were slaves to those that by nature are not gods.
But now that you have come to know God—or rather, to be known by God—how can you turn back again to the weak and destitute elements? Do you want to be slaves to them all over again?
You are observing days and months and seasons and years.
I am afraid for you, that perhaps I have labored over you for nothing.
Become as I am, because I also became as you are—brothers and sisters, I beg you. You did me no wrong.
verse.note: The Greek plural was the normal way to address a mixed group of men and women as siblings, and Paul is writing to whole congregations. “Brothers” alone now suggests to English readers that only men are addressed. Many recent translations make the same choice.

verse.text: You know that it was because of a bodily illness that I first announced the good news to you,
verse.note: The verb was an ordinary word for bringing or proclaiming good news, used also of public and imperial announcements. “Preach the gospel” has become a purely religious phrase in English, so the plainer rendering is used here. Many modern translations alternate between the two.

The Greek expression can mean “the first time,” which would imply Paul had visited the Galatians twice before writing, or simply “originally, back then.” The second, looser sense was common in the period, and the rendering here does not press the first. The question bears on dating the letter and remains disputed.

verse.text: and what was a trial to you in my body you did not scorn or spit at; rather, you welcomed me as an angel of God, as Christ Jesus.
verse.note: The word means a putting to the proof; here Paul’s illness was a hardship that tested how the Galatians would receive him, so “trial” is used and not the older “temptation.” Most modern versions agree. Some manuscripts read “my trial” for “your trial,” which lies behind the King James wording “my temptation which was in my flesh.”

The verb literally means to spit out. Spitting was a common gesture for warding off illness, the evil eye or a demonic influence at the sight of a sick person, and it could also simply express disgust. Many translations paraphrase with “reject” or “loathe”; the literal gesture is kept here because ancient readers would have recognized it.

verse.text: Where then is that blessedness of yours? For I testify to you that, had it been possible, you would have torn out your eyes and given them to me.
So have I become your enemy by telling you the truth?
They are courting you, but not for good; no, they want to shut you out, so that you will court them.

note.traditional: zealously affect; make much of; are zealous for

verse.note: The verb means to be eagerly devoted to someone or to seek them earnestly, whether honorably or not. Paul uses it three times across verses 17 and 18, and “court” is used each time so the repetition can be heard. Other versions have “make much of” or “are zealous to win you over.”

verse.text: Now it is good to be courted in a good cause at all times, and not only when I am present with you,
my children, for whom I am again in labor until Christ is formed in you.
I wish I could be present with you now and change my tone, because I am at a loss about you.
Tell me, you who want to be under the law, do you not listen to the Law?
verse.note: Paul uses the same Greek word twice with a shift of reference. The first means the law of Moses as a regime of commandments; the second means the Law as Scripture, the five books of Moses, from which the Genesis story of Abraham’s two sons is drawn. The capital letter marks the second sense.

verse.text: For it is written that Abraham had two sons, one by the slave woman and one by the free woman.
But the one by the slave woman was born according to the flesh, while the one by the free woman was born through a promise.
These things are said allegorically, for these women are two covenants. One is from Mount Sinai, bearing children for slavery; she is Hagar.
verse.note: The verb can mean either to speak allegorically or to interpret allegorically. Paul may be saying that the Genesis narrative itself points to something further, or that he is now reading it in a figurative way; the Greek allows both. He does not deny that the events happened. He finds in the two women a pattern for two covenants.

verse.text: Now Hagar is Mount Sinai in Arabia and corresponds to the present Jerusalem, for she is in slavery with her children.

note.term: Now Hagar is Mount Sinai in Arabia
note.traditional: For this Agar is mount Sinai in Arabia

verse.note: The manuscripts differ here. Some omit the name Hagar and read “For Sinai is a mountain in Arabia.” The reading translated here identifies Hagar with Sinai, the place where the law was given; scholars are divided over which form is original.

verse.text: But the Jerusalem above is free, and she is our mother.

For it is written: “Rejoice, barren woman who bears no children; break out and shout, you who are not in labor; for the children of the deserted woman are many, more than those of the woman who has a husband.”
Now you, brothers and sisters, are children of promise, like Isaac.
But just as at that time the one born according to the flesh persecuted the one born according to the Spirit, so it is now also.
verse.note: Genesis 21:9 says only that Sarah saw Ishmael “playing” or “laughing,” in the Greek version “playing with Isaac her son.” Jewish interpretive tradition took this as mockery or hostility toward Isaac, and Paul reflects that reading. He sees the same pattern in the pressure his converts now face.

verse.text: But what does the Scripture say? “Throw out the slave woman and her son, for the son of the slave woman will never inherit with the son of the free woman.”
Therefore, brothers and sisters, we are not children of a slave woman but of the free woman.
For freedom Christ set us free. Stand firm, then, and do not let yourselves be held again by a yoke of slavery.

note.traditional: “Stand fast therefore in the liberty wherewith Christ hath made us free” (KJV); “For freedom Christ has set us free” in most modern versions

verse.note: The Greek phrase can mean “for freedom” (the purpose of the liberation) or “by freedom” (its means); the first is the majority view and is followed here. Later manuscripts, followed by the King James Version, attach the phrase to the command instead: “Stand firm in the freedom with which Christ set us free.”

verse.text: Look: I, Paul, tell you that if you let yourselves be circumcised, Christ will be of no benefit to you.
And I testify again to every man who lets himself be circumcised that he is obligated to keep the whole law.
You have been severed from Christ, you who are trying to be justified by law; you have fallen away from grace.

note.traditional: “Christ is become of no effect unto you” (KJV); “severed” or “alienated” in modern versions

verse.note: The verb means to put something out of operation; in the passive with “from” it means to be discharged or cut off from something. The same verb returns in verse 11, where the stumbling block of the cross would be “done away with”. English has no single word that fits both uses.

Greek has one word-family where English has two: “justified” here and “righteousness” in verse 5 share a root, as “just” and “justice” do. The present tense describes an attempt under way, not an accomplished fact, hence “trying to be”.

verse.text: For we, by the Spirit, on the basis of faith, eagerly await the hope of righteousness.
verse.note: The phrase can mean the righteousness that is hoped for, that is, God’s final verdict, or the hope that belongs to those already counted righteous. Most interpreters prefer the first. The rendering is left as open as the Greek.

verse.text: For in Christ Jesus neither circumcision nor uncircumcision counts for anything; what counts is faith working through love.
You were running well. Who cut in on you to keep you from being persuaded by the truth?
verse.note: The verb can mean “obey”, and most translations render it so here. “Persuaded” is used because Paul plays on the same root three times in four verses: being persuaded by the truth (verse 7), “this persuasion” (verse 8) and “I am persuaded” (verse 10). “Obey” hides the link.

verse.text: This persuasion does not come from the one who calls you.
A little leaven leavens the whole batch of dough.
I am persuaded about you in the Lord that you will take no other view. But the one who is troubling you will bear the judgment, whoever he may be.
But as for me, brothers and sisters, if I am still preaching circumcision, why am I still being persecuted? In that case the stumbling block of the cross has been done away with.
I wish those who are unsettling you would go so far as to castrate themselves!

note.traditional: “I would they were even cut off” (KJV); “castrate” or “emasculate” in most modern versions

verse.note: The verb means “cut off”, and it echoes “cut in on” in verse 7. Paul’s bitter joke is that those so eager to cut the foreskin should carry the knife further. Older versions softened this to exclusion from the community, but the reference to castration is the standard scholarly view.

verse.text: For you were called to freedom, brothers and sisters. Only do not let that freedom become an opening for the flesh, but through love be slaves to one another.
verse.note: The verb is the ordinary one for a slave’s service and belongs to the same word-family as “slavery” in verse 1. The paradox is deliberate: those freed from the yoke of slavery are to be slaves to each other through love. Most translations soften it to “serve”, though some have “become slaves”.

In this chapter “flesh” is not the body as such but human nature left to itself, weak and self-centered, as opposed to life directed by God’s Spirit. The list in verses 19–21 includes strife and envy, which are not bodily sins. Some translations paraphrase as “sinful nature”; the traditional word is kept, partly because the letter also uses it of the literal flesh cut in circumcision.

verse.text: For the whole law is fulfilled in a single saying: “You shall love your neighbor as yourself.”
But if you bite and devour one another, watch out that you are not consumed by one another.
But I say: walk by the Spirit, and you will never carry out the desire of the flesh.
For the flesh sets its desire against the Spirit, and the Spirit against the flesh; these are opposed to each other, so that you do not do whatever you want.

note.term: so that you do not do whatever you want
note.traditional: so that ye cannot do the things that ye would

verse.note: The clause may express the result of the conflict or its purpose. “Whatever you want” may be the good a person wishes to do, which the flesh blocks; the evil the flesh craves, which the Spirit blocks; or both. Interpreters are divided, and the rendering does not decide between them.

verse.text: But if you are led by the Spirit, you are not under law.
Now the works of the flesh are obvious: sexual immorality, impurity, debauchery,
idolatry, sorcery, hostilities, strife, jealousy, outbursts of rage, selfish rivalries, dissensions, factions,
envy, drunkenness, carousing, and things like these. About these I tell you in advance, just as I told you before, that those who practice such things will not inherit the kingdom of God.
verse.note: Many later manuscripts add “murders” after “envy”; the two Greek words look and sound alike. The King James Version includes it. Important early manuscripts lack it, and the SBLGNT text translated here omits it.

verse.text: But the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faithfulness,
verse.note: This is the same Greek word translated “faith” in verses 5 and 6. In a list of qualities shown toward other people, it most likely means reliability or trustworthiness, and most modern translations agree. Some interpreters take it as trust in God.

verse.text: gentleness, self-control. Against such things there is no law.
verse.note: “Meekness” now suggests weakness or timidity, which the Greek word does not. It describes someone who is not harsh or self-assertive. “Gentleness” is the usual rendering in modern translations.

verse.text: And those who belong to Christ have crucified the flesh with its passions and desires.
If we live by the Spirit, let us also keep in step with the Spirit.
Let us not become conceited, provoking one another, envying one another.

Brothers and sisters, even if a person is caught in some offense, you who are spiritual should restore such a person in a spirit of gentleness—each of you watching yourself, so that you too are not tempted.
verse.note: The Greek plural was the ordinary way to address a mixed group of men and women, and Paul is writing to whole congregations. Older versions have “brethren” or “brothers”; many recent translations now render it “brothers and sisters” for the same reason.

The verb can mean that the person is detected by others in the act, or that the person is overtaken by the offense, caught off guard by it. “Caught in” leaves both possibilities open. Commentators are divided, though the gentle tone of the verse fits the idea of someone taken by surprise.

The word means a wrongful act, a moral failure. “Trespass” is the traditional rendering, but in current English it mainly suggests entering property without permission. English versions vary among “trespass”, “transgression”, “sin” and “offense”; the meaning itself is not disputed.

Older versions have “a spirit of meekness”. “Meek” now suggests weakness or timidity, which the Greek word does not; it describes a gentle, unassertive way of dealing with others. “Gentleness” is the usual rendering in modern translations.

verse.text: Carry one another’s burdens, and in this way you will fulfill the law of Christ.
For if anyone thinks they are something when they are nothing, they are deluding themselves.
But let each person examine their own work, and then they will have their reason to boast in themselves alone and not in someone else,
for each person will carry their own load.
verse.note: Paul uses a different word here from the “burdens” of verse 2, and the translation keeps them distinct. Verse 2 concerns weights that others can help carry. This verse, following the call to self-examination, concerns the responsibility each person has for their own work, most likely with God’s final assessment in view. Older versions use “burden” in both places, which makes the two statements seem to conflict.

verse.text: The one who is instructed in the word should share all good things with the one who instructs.
verse.note: The verb is the ordinary one for sharing or partnership, and Paul uses related language elsewhere for financial support. Most interpreters take the verse as an instruction that those who receive teaching should support their teachers materially. “All good things” may be broader than money.

verse.text: Do not be deceived: God is not mocked. For whatever a person sows, that they will also reap,
because the one who sows to their own flesh will reap decay from the flesh, but the one who sows to the Spirit will reap eternal life from the Spirit.
verse.note: The word means decay, ruin or destruction, the rotting of what perishes, and here it stands as the opposite of eternal life. “Corruption” is the traditional rendering, but in modern English it chiefly suggests dishonesty or bribery. Some versions have “destruction”.

verse.text: Let us not grow weary of doing what is right, for at the proper time we will reap, if we do not give up.
So then, while we have time, let us do good to everyone, and especially to those who belong to the household of the faith.
See what large letters I am writing to you with my own hand.

note.traditional: how large a letter / what large letters

verse.note: Letters were normally dictated to a secretary, and the sender often added a closing in his own handwriting to authenticate it. Paul appears to take the pen at this point, though some think the remark covers the whole letter. Why his writing was large is unknown: emphasis, an unpracticed hand and poor eyesight have all been suggested. The King James “how large a letter” (a long epistle) is not what the Greek says.

verse.text: Those who want to make a good showing in the flesh are the ones trying to compel you to be circumcised—only so that they will not be persecuted for the cross of Christ.
For not even those who are circumcised keep the law themselves; they want you to be circumcised so that they may boast in your flesh.
verse.note: The Greek is a present participle, which could mean “those who are circumcised” as a class (the people pressing for circumcision) or “those who are getting themselves circumcised” (converts who accept the rite). Some manuscripts read a perfect participle, “those who have been circumcised”. Most interpreters take it as a reference to the advocates of circumcision themselves.

verse.text: But as for me, may I never boast except in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ, through which the world has been crucified to me, and I to the world.
verse.note: The Greek pronoun can refer either to the cross (“through which”) or to Jesus Christ (“through whom”). Most modern translations choose the cross, since it is the object of the boasting and the next clause speaks of crucifixion. The King James has “by whom”. The sense differs little either way.

verse.text: For neither circumcision nor uncircumcision is anything; what matters is a new creation.
And as for all who will keep in step with this rule—peace be upon them, and mercy, and upon the Israel of God.

note.term: and upon the Israel of God
note.traditional: and upon the Israel of God

verse.note: This phrase is among the most disputed in the letter. The “and” may be explanatory (“that is, the Israel of God”), identifying all who follow this rule, Jew and Gentile alike, as God’s Israel. Or it may add a distinct group: Jewish believers, or the Jewish people for whom Paul wishes mercy. The translation keeps the Greek word order and the plain “and” so that both readings remain open.

verse.text: From now on, let no one cause me trouble, for I carry the marks of Jesus on my body.

note.traditional: marks of the Lord Jesus / marks of Jesus

verse.note: The word was used for marks tattooed or branded on the body, especially those that identified a slave’s owner or a devotee’s god. Paul most likely means the scars left by beatings and stonings suffered in his work, which show whose servant he is. The later use of “stigmata” for wounds corresponding to those of the crucifixion is not in view.

verse.text: The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with your spirit, brothers and sisters. Amen.
